title: War & Peace Theory
description: Causes of war, just war tradition, democratic peace

concepts.title: Causes of War: Realism, Liberalism, Constructivism
concepts.contentHtml:
The scholarly study of war's causes has produced several major theoretical traditions. Realism, traceable to Thucydides and Machiavelli but systematised by 20th-century thinkers including Hans Morgenthau and Kenneth Waltz, treats war as a recurring feature of an anarchic international system in which states must look out for their own security. Kenneth Waltz's Theory of International Politics (1979) developed the structural-realist account: the absence of any authority above states forces them into self-help behaviour; the resulting security dilemma (defensive measures by one state appear threatening to others) makes war recurrent regardless of states' intentions.

Liberalism in international-relations theory emphasises the conditions that reduce war's probability. Immanuel Kant's Perpetual Peace (1795) identified the conditions for durable peace: republican government, federation of free states, cosmopolitan right. The 20th- and 21st-century liberal-IR tradition has extended Kant's analysis through extensive empirical work on the democratic peace hypothesis, the role of international institutions, and the pacifying effects of trade and economic interdependence.

Constructivism in IR theory, developed by Alexander Wendt (Social Theory of International Politics, 1999) and others, emphasises that international politics is socially constructed rather than determined by material conditions alone. States' interests are shaped by their identities, which are themselves shaped by social interaction. Wendt's slogan, 'anarchy is what states make of it,' captures the constructivist position: the realist account assumes a particular kind of social structure rather than describing an inevitable feature of international life.

concepts.title: The Just War Tradition
concepts.contentHtml:
The just war tradition — the body of moral and legal thought analysing when war is justified and how it must be conducted — is one of the oldest sustained traditions of moral philosophy. The tradition runs through Augustine's 5th-century theological reflections on Christian participation in just wars, Thomas Aquinas's 13th-century systematic articulation, the early-modern Spanish scholastics (Vitoria, Suárez), Hugo Grotius's foundational De Jure Belli ac Pacis (1625), and continuing 20th-century elaborations by writers including Michael Walzer (Just and Unjust Wars, 1977).

The tradition distinguishes jus ad bellum (the criteria for when war is justified) from jus in bello (the criteria for how war must be conducted). The standard jus ad bellum criteria include: just cause (war must respond to actual injury or imminent threat); right intention (war must aim at restoring just peace, not at conquest or revenge); legitimate authority (only competent political authorities may declare war); last resort (other means of redress must have been exhausted); reasonable prospect of success; and proportionality (the harms war will cause must not exceed the goods it can secure). The jus in bello criteria emphasise discrimination (combatants and civilians must be distinguished, with civilians not directly targeted) and proportionality in specific military operations.

The tradition's contemporary application has been substantial. The 2003 Iraq War provoked extensive just-war analysis (most concluding the war did not meet just-cause criteria); the 2008–2009 Gaza conflict produced sustained debate over jus in bello proportionality; the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine has been widely classified as a clear case of unjust aggression; the post-October-7 Israel-Hamas conflict has produced intense debate over both jus ad bellum and jus in bello dimensions. The tradition does not produce determinate answers in many hard cases — reasonable people applying its criteria carefully reach different conclusions — but it provides the standard moral vocabulary in which contemporary war debates take place.

concepts.title: The Democratic Peace and Its Limits
concepts.contentHtml:
One of the most-discussed empirical findings in international-relations theory is the democratic peace hypothesis: the observation that mature liberal democracies have not fought wars against each other for nearly two centuries. The empirical pattern was identified by Michael Doyle in influential 1983 articles drawing on Kant's Perpetual Peace and has been documented and debated extensively since.

The proposed mechanisms include: institutional (democratic accountability and the costs of war for elected leaders), cultural (shared liberal-democratic norms producing trust between democracies), and structural (economic interdependence and shared institutions). The empirical pattern is strong but not absolute — disagreements continue over how to define 'democracy' (the cases that count as democracies have been debated case by case), what counts as 'war' between democracies, and whether the pattern reflects causal mechanisms or selection effects.

The contemporary qualifications matter. The democratic peace concerns full democracies, not partial or hybrid regimes (which on some analyses have higher war rates than either democracies or autocracies). The post-2010 wave of democratic backsliding has reduced the share of countries that qualify as 'full' democracies on common measures. The contemporary US-China rivalry, the Russia-NATO standoff, and the broader fracturing of post-1989 institutional cooperation have raised questions about whether the conditions that produced the democratic peace will persist. The empirical claim — democracies haven't fought each other much in the past 200 years — is robust; the predictive claim — democracies will continue not to fight each other — is much more uncertain.

title: Nuclear Deterrence & Strategy
description: MAD, second-strike, proliferation, arms control — the bomb's logic

concepts.title: From Hiroshima to MAD
concepts.contentHtml:
The August 1945 American atomic bombings of Hiroshima (August 6, around 70,000 immediate deaths, 140,000 by year-end including radiation) and Nagasaki (August 9, around 40,000 immediate, 70,000 by year-end) initiated the nuclear age. The Soviet Union's August 1949 first nuclear test ended the American monopoly; Britain (1952), France (1960), China (1964), India (1974), Israel (probably mid-1960s but never officially declared), Pakistan (1998), and North Korea (2006) followed in subsequent decades.

The 1950s development of thermonuclear weapons (the hydrogen bomb, with yields hundreds to thousands of times larger than fission weapons), intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs), and submarine-launched ballistic missiles (SLBMs) produced the nuclear triad — land-based missiles, submarine-launched missiles, and strategic bombers — that gave nuclear powers diverse second-strike capabilities. The doctrinal consequence was Mutual Assured Destruction (MAD): if two nuclear powers each have second-strike capability, neither can win a nuclear war, so neither would rationally start one.

The strategic-studies tradition developed elaborate analyses of how nuclear deterrence works. Bernard Brodie, Thomas Schelling, Albert Wohlstetter, Henry Kissinger, and others contributed to the post-war literature on deterrence stability, escalation control, limited nuclear war, and crisis bargaining. Schelling's The Strategy of Conflict (1960) and Arms and Influence (1966) became foundational texts. The combination of game-theoretic rigor with policy relevance gave nuclear strategy a distinctive intellectual character that has continued to shape thinking about deterrence in non-nuclear contexts.

concepts.title: Nuclear Crises and Arms Control
concepts.contentHtml:
The Cold War produced multiple nuclear crises that tested deterrence theory in practice. The Cuban Missile Crisis (October 1962), in which the discovery of Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba produced the closest moment to nuclear war in the post-1945 period, has been studied extensively as a case in crisis management, decision-making under pressure, and the role of luck in deterrence stability. The 1983 Able Archer NATO exercise nearly produced Soviet preemptive action against what Soviet intelligence interpreted as actual war preparation. The 1995 Norwegian Black Brant rocket incident saw Yeltsin briefed on a possible US nuclear attack before the missile's actual scientific purpose was identified.

The arms-control infrastructure built up over the Cold War limited the size and character of nuclear arsenals. The Limited Test Ban Treaty (1963), the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT, 1968), the SALT I and II treaties, the INF Treaty (1987, eliminating intermediate-range nuclear missiles in Europe), the START series of strategic-arms-reduction treaties, and the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (1996, signed but not ratified by major powers including the US) collectively constrained the nuclear competition.

The contemporary nuclear environment is more dangerous than at any point since the late Cold War. The 2002 US withdrawal from the ABM Treaty, the 2019 collapse of the INF Treaty, the 2023 Russian suspension of New START participation, the post-2014 deterioration of US-Russian strategic dialogue, the modernisation programmes by all major nuclear powers, the continuing North Korean nuclear-weapons programme, and the prospect of Iranian nuclear weapons all contribute to the breakdown of the post-1989 arms-control framework. Whether a new arms-control architecture emerges or the existing framework continues to erode is one of the central security-policy questions of the period.

concepts.title: Proliferation and Future Concerns
concepts.contentHtml:
The proliferation question — whether, when, and how additional states acquire nuclear weapons — has been the major non-superpower nuclear-policy concern. The 1968 NPT attempted to limit proliferation through a bargain: existing nuclear powers committed to disarmament; non-nuclear-weapon states committed not to acquire nuclear weapons; all parties committed to peaceful nuclear cooperation. The bargain has been imperfect — existing nuclear powers have not seriously disarmed, the peaceful-cooperation pillar has produced civilian programmes that complicate non-proliferation enforcement, and the IAEA's monitoring role has had to be supplemented by intelligence and political-military pressure to detect actual weapons programmes.

The India-Pakistan case (both 1998 declared, with Israeli assistance for India's earlier programme), the North Korean case (continuing programme producing dozens of weapons by 2024), and the protracted Iran negotiations (the 2015 JCPOA agreement and its 2018 US withdrawal) illustrate the continuing challenge. The 2003 Libya disarmament and the 2011 Libya intervention have widely been read as a cautionary tale for North Korean and Iranian leaderships about the costs of giving up nuclear capabilities; whether that reading was correct is contested but politically consequential.

The future concerns include the possibility of new state proliferators (Saudi Arabia, South Korea, Turkey, perhaps Japan if regional security deteriorates), non-state nuclear acquisition (which has not happened but cannot be ruled out), and the implications of artificial intelligence for nuclear command-and-control. The combination of degraded arms-control architecture, modernising arsenals, and new technologies makes the contemporary nuclear environment potentially more dangerous than the late Cold War's relatively stable bipolar deterrence. The honest assessment is that we are in a more uncertain nuclear era than at any time since the early 1980s, and the institutional response has not been adequate to the level of risk.

concepts.title: Defining Terrorism and Its History
concepts.contentHtml:
Terrorism is one of the most politically-loaded categories in security studies. The standard scholarly definition emphasises four features: violence or threat of violence, political motivation, non-state actors (though the category of state terrorism complicates this), and targeting of civilians or non-combatants for psychological effect. The familiar slogan 'one person's terrorist is another's freedom fighter' captures both the genuine difficulty of categorisation and the political stakes of the labels themselves.

The historical sweep is older than the term itself. The first-century Sicarii (Jewish daggermen targeting Roman collaborators); the 9th–13th-century Assassins (Nizari Ismaili sect); the 19th-century anarchist wave that assassinated heads of state including Lincoln (1865), Tsar Alexander II (1881), Empress Elisabeth of Austria (1898), King Umberto I of Italy (1900), and President McKinley (1901); the early-20th-century anti-colonial and revolutionary movements — all illustrate that politically-motivated targeting of authority figures and broader populations has been a recurring feature of political conflict.

The 20th-century wave produced multiple distinct phases. Anti-colonial terrorism in the 1950s and 1960s (the Algerian FLN, the Mau Mau in Kenya, the Vietminh, the Provisional IRA's earlier phase). Left-wing European terrorism in the 1970s (the Red Brigades in Italy, the Red Army Faction in Germany, the Direct Action group in France). Religious-nationalist terrorism through the late 20th century (Hamas, Hezbollah, the various Sikh militant groups in 1980s India). Salafi-jihadist terrorism rising from the 1990s through al-Qaeda, the post-9/11 transnational jihadi movement, and Islamic State at its 2014–2017 peak. Each wave had distinctive ideological and operational characters; treating them as a single phenomenon obscures more than it illuminates.

concepts.title: 9/11 and the Post-2001 Counter-Terrorism Era
concepts.contentHtml:
The September 11, 2001 attacks killed 2,977 people in New York, Washington, and Pennsylvania and produced the most consequential single security event of the post-Cold-War period. The subsequent 'Global War on Terror' shaped two decades of US and allied foreign policy. The Afghan campaign began in October 2001; the Iraq War in March 2003; the broader counter-terrorism campaign extended across multiple theatres including Yemen, Somalia, the Philippines, the trans-Sahel region, and many others. The cumulative cost — financial (estimates of $5–8 trillion in direct US costs alone), human (over 7,000 American military deaths, perhaps 800,000 deaths in Iraq, Afghanistan, Pakistan, Syria, and Yemen across post-9/11 conflicts), and political (the post-9/11 expansion of surveillance powers, the use of torture and detention without trial, the Iraq War's contribution to anti-American sentiment) — has been one of the major historical events of the early 21st century.

The institutional response built up over the post-9/11 period was substantial. The US Department of Homeland Security (2002), the expanded NSA mass-surveillance programmes revealed by Edward Snowden in 2013, the development of armed drone capabilities and their use in targeted killings across multiple countries, the post-2007 'surge' counterinsurgency doctrines associated with David Petraeus and others, and the much-expanded special-operations forces are among the institutional changes. Most have proved remarkably durable; despite the formal end of US combat operations in Iraq and Afghanistan, much of the post-9/11 counter-terrorism apparatus continues to operate.

The scholarly assessment of the post-9/11 era has been substantially critical. The Iraq War's failure of just-war and strategic judgement; the abuse of detainees including the systematic torture programme run by the CIA from 2002 to 2009 (documented by the Senate Intelligence Committee report, 2014); the continuing operation of the Guantánamo detention facility; the post-2021 Afghan collapse demonstrating that two decades of counterinsurgency had not built durable Afghan state capacity. The combination has produced widespread re-evaluation of the post-9/11 strategic choices, and the political coalition supporting expansive counter-terrorism operations has substantially eroded.

concepts.title: Counterinsurgency and Asymmetric Warfare
concepts.contentHtml:
Counterinsurgency (COIN) is the broader category of military operations aimed at defeating insurgent movements. The intellectual tradition runs through the British Malayan Emergency (1948–1960), the French Algerian War (1954–1962, ultimately lost despite tactical successes), the American counterinsurgency in Vietnam (also lost), and the post-9/11 American doctrine articulated in FM 3-24 Counterinsurgency (2006, under David Petraeus). The 2007 'surge' in Iraq applied the doctrine with apparent tactical success that did not translate into political success.

The classic COIN framework distinguishes the population-centric from the enemy-centric approaches. Population-centric COIN emphasises winning popular support — security for the population, governance reforms, economic development, political negotiation — as the foundation for defeating insurgency. Enemy-centric COIN emphasises directly targeting insurgent forces and infrastructure. The doctrinal consensus in the post-9/11 period favoured population-centric approaches; the empirical results were mixed at best, and the post-2021 Afghan collapse has substantially undermined confidence in the doctrine's strategic effectiveness in long-term occupations of foreign territory.

The asymmetric-warfare framework analyses how weaker actors with limited military capabilities can effectively contest stronger ones through avoiding pitched battles, targeting symbolic and economic targets, leveraging information operations, and exploiting the political costs that protracted conflict imposes on stronger actors. Mao Zedong's On Guerrilla Warfare (1937) and Che Guevara's Guerrilla Warfare (1961) are foundational texts in the strategic-doctrine tradition. The contemporary application — Ukrainian asymmetric tactics against Russian forces, Houthi Red Sea operations against shipping, Hezbollah's deterrence-through-escalation framework against Israel — illustrates how the basic logic continues to apply across very different specific contexts.

title: Cyber & Hybrid Conflict
description: Information warfare, gray zone, cyber operations, election interference

concepts.title: The Cyber Domain and Strategic Logic
concepts.contentHtml:
The development of cyber operations as an instrument of statecraft has been one of the major security-policy developments of the past two decades. The first major recognised state cyber operation — the 2007 Russian cyber attack on Estonia following the Tallinn statue dispute — demonstrated that cyber instruments could produce political effects independent of conventional military capability. The 2010 Stuxnet operation, attributed to a US-Israeli partnership, demonstrated that cyber operations could produce kinetic-equivalent effects, sabotaging Iranian nuclear-enrichment centrifuges through targeted malware.

The strategic logic of cyber operations differs from kinetic-conflict logic in several ways. Attribution is harder — sophisticated operations can be conducted with substantial anonymity. Cost asymmetry favours offence — capable cyber operations require substantially less investment than kinetic capabilities of comparable strategic effect. Effects can range from temporary service disruption through to permanent destruction of physical equipment. Escalation dynamics are uncertain — there are no settled doctrines for how cyber operations interact with kinetic conflict.

The major state cyber actors include the United States (NSA's Tailored Access Operations, US Cyber Command), Russia (the GRU's Unit 26165, the Sandworm group, the SVR's APT29 Cozy Bear group), China (PLA Unit 61398, the broader Ministry of State Security cyber operations), North Korea (the Lazarus Group, responsible for the 2014 Sony hack and the 2017 WannaCry ransomware), Iran, and Israel (Unit 8200, partner in Stuxnet). Beyond states, criminal cyber operations (ransomware groups including Conti, REvil, BlackCat) and cyber-mercenary operations (NSO Group's Pegasus spyware) operate at scales that complicate the state-vs-non-state distinction.

concepts.title: Hybrid Warfare and the Gray Zone
concepts.contentHtml:
The category of hybrid warfare describes the integrated use of conventional military force, irregular tactics, cyber operations, information warfare, economic coercion, and political subversion to achieve strategic effects below the threshold of conventional war. The concept was developed by NATO analysts in the 2000s and accelerated in use after the 2014 Russian operations in Crimea and eastern Ukraine, which combined deniable special-operations forces (the 'little green men'), cyber operations, energy-leverage threats, and an extensive disinformation campaign in a coordinated effort.

The 'gray zone' framing emphasises the strategic use of activity below the conventional war threshold to achieve goals that direct military action would also pursue. Chinese coast-guard and maritime-militia operations in the South China Sea; Russian assassination operations on Western soil (the Litvinenko poisoning, 2006; Skripal poisoning, 2018; the Berlin Tiergarten killing, 2019); Iranian proxy operations through Hezbollah, the Houthis, and various Iraqi and Syrian militias; North Korean abductions of Japanese citizens and similar operations — all illustrate the broad use of gray-zone tactics across major state actors.

The defensive challenge for democracies and rules-based international institutions is substantial. Conventional military responses to gray-zone provocations risk escalation; cyber responses face attribution and proportionality difficulties; sanctions responses are slow and partially effective; legal-institutional responses face the asymmetry that authoritarian states do not face equivalent constraints. The post-2014 NATO and EU responses have built up significant new institutional capacity (the European Centre of Excellence for Countering Hybrid Threats in Helsinki, NATO's hybrid-warfare doctrines, the EU's StratCom East task force) but have not solved the underlying asymmetry.

concepts.title: Election Interference and Information Operations
concepts.contentHtml:
Election interference has become one of the most-studied dimensions of contemporary hybrid conflict. The 2016 Russian operations against the US election (covered in detail in the media-misinformation topic) combined hacking and dumping (DCCC and DNC email leaks through WikiLeaks), social-media disinformation through the Internet Research Agency, attempted intrusion into election infrastructure, and broader divisive-content amplification. The Mueller investigation, the Senate Intelligence Committee reports, and subsequent academic and journalistic work have documented the operations in detail; the political consequences have been complicated by the partisan polarisation of US responses.

The pattern has continued and expanded. Russian operations against the 2017 French election (the Macron Leaks); the 2024 European Parliament elections; the Romanian first-round annulled election of late 2024; multiple national elections worldwide have featured documented foreign-influence operations. Chinese operations have expanded to target Taiwanese, Australian, Canadian, and US elections at smaller but growing scale. Iranian operations have been documented in the 2020 and 2024 US elections.

The defensive responses have been imperfect. Platform-level interventions (Meta's threat-disruption operations, Twitter/X's reduced moderation under Musk, Google's Threat Analysis Group) have mixed effectiveness. Government-coordination institutions (the now-reduced US Global Engagement Center, the UK Counter Disinformation Cell, the EU Disinfo Lab) have produced incremental improvement. Election-security investments at state and federal level in the US have improved physical-infrastructure security but produced limited progress on social-media-driven information operations. The fundamental asymmetry — that operating an influence campaign costs less than detecting and neutralising one — remains unresolved, and the AI-generation technologies covered in earlier topics tilt that asymmetry further toward attackers.

title: Intelligence & Espionage
description: HUMINT, SIGINT, OSINT — the secret machinery of statecraft

concepts.title: Intelligence Disciplines and Their Trade-Offs
concepts.contentHtml:
The professional intelligence community organises its work around several distinct collection disciplines. Human intelligence (HUMINT) — collected through human sources, including agents, defectors, and clandestine officers — has been the canonical intelligence form for centuries and remains crucial for political-leadership intentions, organisational dynamics, and topics that lend themselves to interpretation. Signals intelligence (SIGINT) — communications intelligence and electronic intelligence collected from electromagnetic emissions — has been the dominant US intelligence-collection investment since the Cold War, conducted at scale by the National Security Agency. Geospatial intelligence (GEOINT) — imagery and analysis from satellites and aerial platforms — has become increasingly important with the proliferation of high-resolution commercial imagery.

Open-source intelligence (OSINT) — analysis of publicly-available information including social media, commercial databases, news media, and academic publications — has grown enormously in the digital era. The OSINT-focused journalism organisations including Bellingcat (founded 2014 by Eliot Higgins) have produced major investigations on the MH17 shootdown, Russian assassination operations, and Syrian chemical-weapons use that traditional state intelligence services would have struggled to produce or to share publicly. The democratisation of OSINT has shifted some traditional intelligence functions toward civilian and journalistic actors.

The collection-discipline trade-offs matter operationally. HUMINT can produce unique insights but is risky for sources, slow to develop, and unreliable in many environments. SIGINT can produce vast quantities of information but has bulk-vs-targeted-collection trade-offs and depends on continuing access to communications systems. GEOINT and OSINT can provide ground truth but have limitations in interpreting intent. The professional intelligence services balance these disciplines based on resources, target-specific feasibility, and operational priorities; the analytical task of integrating different collection streams into actionable intelligence is one of the central skills of the profession.

concepts.title: The Major Intelligence Services
concepts.contentHtml:
The post-1945 development of large state intelligence services has produced one of the most substantial institutional expansions of any state function. The US intelligence community includes the CIA (founded 1947), the NSA (1952), the DIA (Defense Intelligence Agency, 1961), the National Reconnaissance Office (1961), the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency (1996), and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (2004) coordinating across them. Total US intelligence spending — much of it classified — is estimated at over $80 billion annually.

The UK intelligence services — MI6 / SIS (foreign intelligence), MI5 / Security Service (domestic security), GCHQ (signals intelligence) — operate at smaller but still substantial scale. The Five Eyes (US, UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand) intelligence-sharing alliance, dating to wartime cooperation, remains the most extensive such arrangement and produces shared SIGINT and analytical product across the partner services.

The major adversary services include Russia's FSB (domestic security and counter-intelligence), SVR (foreign intelligence, the post-1991 successor to the KGB's First Chief Directorate), and GRU (military intelligence). China's Ministry of State Security (MSS) and the PLA's intelligence units. Israel's Mossad, Shin Bet, and military intelligence (Aman). Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security and the Quds Force of the IRGC. North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau. Each operates within distinctive legal frameworks, organisational cultures, and operational priorities; treating them as institutionally homogeneous obscures the actual variation.

concepts.title: Failures, Reforms, and Democratic Oversight
concepts.contentHtml:
Intelligence services have produced a long history of high-profile failures. The 1961 Bay of Pigs operation; the failure to anticipate the 1973 Yom Kippur War; the failure to anticipate the 1979 Iranian Revolution; the failure to anticipate the 1989 collapse of communist regimes; the 2002 NIE on Iraqi WMD that supported the 2003 invasion; the failure to anticipate the rise of ISIS in 2014; the recent debates over Russia's pre-2022 Ukraine invasion intentions. Each failure has produced post-mortems, reform efforts, and the next generation of expectations about what intelligence services can and cannot do.

The oversight of intelligence services in democracies has been one of the most consequential institutional challenges. The post-Watergate Church Committee investigations (1975) produced the modern US framework: the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence; the FISA Court's oversight of foreign-intelligence surveillance; the inspectors-general systems for individual agencies. The framework has had mixed results. The 2013 Snowden disclosures revealed mass-surveillance programmes that had been authorised through secret legal interpretations and that congressional overseers had imperfect knowledge of. Subsequent reforms have improved transparency but the fundamental tension between effective intelligence operations and democratic accountability remains.

The contemporary stress on intelligence-democracy relationships has intensified. The post-2020 US politicisation of intelligence — accusations of 'deep state' operations, the politicised handling of intelligence leaks, the 2025 reorganisation of US intelligence agencies — illustrates how intelligence services can become political objects in ways that complicate their professional functioning. The British intelligence-services reforms following Iraq, the multiple French parliamentary commissions on intelligence oversight, and the German constitutional-court rulings on BND foreign-surveillance practices illustrate that the underlying problems are general rather than US-specific. Whether democratic intelligence services can maintain effective operations alongside meaningful accountability is one of the continuing central problems of intelligence governance.

title: Civil War & Insurgency
description: Greed vs grievance, ethnic conflict, post-conflict reconstruction

concepts.title: What Causes Civil Wars
concepts.contentHtml:
Civil war — armed conflict within a state, typically defined as having at least 1,000 battle deaths over a year — has been the dominant form of large-scale armed conflict in the post-1945 period. The post-1945 number of state-versus-state wars has fallen substantially; the number of civil wars has not. The shift reflects multiple factors: the consolidation of the international state system, the costs of inter-state war for nuclear-armed and conventionally-capable states, and the proliferation of new states with weaker domestic political institutions.

The academic literature on civil-war causation has produced several major waves. The 'greed vs grievance' debate launched by Paul Collier and Anke Hoeffler's influential papers (from 1998) initially seemed to suggest that grievances (ethnic discrimination, repression, inequality) were less important than 'greed' (opportunities for armed groups to fund themselves through resource extraction or extortion). Subsequent work has substantially complicated this finding: greed and grievance interact, and the relative importance varies by case.

The contemporary consensus, drawing on extensive empirical work by Stathis Kalyvas, James Fearon, David Laitin, and others, emphasises several recurring conditions. State weakness (low capacity to suppress armed challenges); opportunity for armed mobilisation (rough terrain, sanctuary across borders, available weapons); fundable opportunities (resource wealth that can sustain armed groups); previous conflict (the strongest predictor of civil war is having had a recent civil war); and ethnic polarisation (especially in combination with political exclusion of large ethnic groups). Single-cause explanations have been undermined by the empirical evidence; the multi-causal accounts are inevitably less satisfying narratively but better-supported.

concepts.title: Major Cases and Patterns
concepts.contentHtml:
The post-1945 civil-war record includes several major cases that have shaped the literature. The Chinese Civil War (1945–1949) produced the People's Republic and shaped subsequent communist-revolution models. The Vietnam War (1955–1975, depending on definitions) became the canonical cold-war proxy conflict. The Nigerian-Biafran war (1967–1970) was an early African case combining ethnic mobilisation with resource-control issues. The Lebanese Civil War (1975–1990) showed how religious-sectarian cleavages could sustain protracted multi-faction conflict. The post-1989 Yugoslav wars (1991–2001) produced ethnic-cleansing campaigns and the genocide at Srebrenica (1995). The Rwandan genocide (1994) killed an estimated 800,000 in 100 days. The post-2003 Iraqi insurgency and the Syrian Civil War (from 2011) have produced some of the largest armed conflicts of the past 25 years.

The contemporary set of active civil wars and insurgencies is substantial: Ukraine (post-2014, escalated 2022); Syria (2011–); Yemen (2015–); Myanmar (post-2021 coup); Sudan (post-2023 conflict); the Sahel region (Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger); the Democratic Republic of the Congo (continuing conflict in eastern provinces); Ethiopia's Tigray war (2020–2022) and continuing Amhara insurgency. The Uppsala Conflict Data Programme documents the world's active armed conflicts; the post-2010 trend has been a substantial increase in the number of state-based armed conflicts, reversing a decline that had characterised the immediate post-Cold-War period.

The scholarly findings on duration are striking. Civil wars typically last much longer than inter-state wars — median duration is around seven years, with many cases lasting decades. Negotiated settlements are harder to reach and to sustain than military victories. Post-conflict reversion to violence is common; Barbara Walter's work has documented that perhaps 40% of negotiated civil-war settlements break down within five years. The combination produces the recurring pattern of multi-decade conflicts (the Colombian armed conflict from 1964 to the 2016 peace agreement; the various phases of Afghan conflict from 1978 to the present) that have produced cumulative human costs comparable to major inter-state wars.

concepts.title: Post-Conflict Reconstruction and the Resilience Problem
concepts.contentHtml:
The challenge of post-conflict reconstruction has been one of the central questions of post-Cold-War security policy. The major attempts — Bosnia after Dayton (1995), Kosovo after 1999, post-2001 Afghanistan, post-2003 Iraq, post-2003 Liberia, post-2007 Sierra Leone, post-2011 South Sudan — have produced mixed results. The successful cases (Bosnia in security terms despite continuing political dysfunction; Sierra Leone's relative consolidation; East Timor's eventual stabilisation) have generally featured sustained international engagement, capable local political coalitions, and underlying conditions favourable to consolidation. The failures (Afghanistan, Iraq, Libya, South Sudan) have featured one or more of: insufficient international commitment; absent or weak local political coalitions; underlying conditions (state weakness, ethnic polarisation, regional spoilers) that made consolidation difficult.

The practical question of how to reduce the recurrence of civil wars has produced a substantial empirical and policy literature. Demobilisation, disarmament, and reintegration (DDR) programmes for former combatants have been one of the major operational interventions; the empirical evidence on their effectiveness is mixed. Security-sector reform programmes have similarly mixed records. Transitional justice mechanisms — the South African Truth and Reconciliation Commission, the various international and hybrid criminal tribunals (ICTY for Yugoslavia, ICTR for Rwanda, the Special Court for Sierra Leone) — have produced important accountability work but uncertain effects on long-run political stability.

The fundamental resilience problem is that the underlying conditions that produced civil war (weak state capacity, ethnic polarisation, economic stagnation) are often not addressed by post-conflict interventions. The Hartzell-Hoddie work on durable settlements identifies institutional power-sharing arrangements (territorial autonomy for distinct ethnic groups, military integration, formal political-power-sharing) as the most reliable structural feature of stable post-conflict settlements. The 1995 Dayton Accords and the 1998 Good Friday Agreement (Northern Ireland) are major positive examples. The post-2024 deterioration of multiple long-frozen conflicts (Nagorno-Karabakh resolution by Azerbaijani military force in 2023; the Sudan conflict eruption in 2023; multiple Sahel breakdowns) illustrate how fragile even apparently-stable post-conflict settlements can be. The honest assessment is that civil-war prevention and post-conflict consolidation are among the hardest problems in international politics, and the post-Cold-War record is one of substantial effort with mixed results.
